1 | # Agent Orchestration Design
2 | 
3 | ## Overview
4 | 
5 | sdlc-harness runs four P0 governance agents inside a single Bob session under
6 | the `🔧 SDLC Harness` mode. This document covers how each agent is triggered,
7 | how they share context within a session, and how conflicts between their
8 | suggestions are surfaced to the user.
9 | 
10 | ---
11 | 
12 | ## The Four P0 Agents (+ P1 slot)
13 | 
14 | | ID | Agent | Concern |
15 | |---|---|---|
16 | | AC | Acceptance-criteria | Issues without Given-When-Then AC |
17 | | AM | Ambiguity detection | Issues with vague or contradictory descriptions |
18 | | DEP | Dependency suggestion | Issues that likely block or relate to each other |
19 | | ST | State-transition | Issues whose GitLab state is stale relative to activity |
20 | | TC *(P1)* | Test-coverage linkage | Issues with no linked test file or test-plan item |
21 | 
22 | ---
23 | 
24 | ## Trigger model
25 | 
26 | All four agents are **on-demand / user-initiated** for the MVP demo. There is no
27 | background polling daemon. The user activates the `🔧 SDLC Harness` mode,
28 | invokes the skill with a prompt (e.g. "audit the backlog" or "check issue #12
29 | for missing AC"), and Bob runs the relevant agent(s) synchronously inside that
30 | chat session.
31 | 
32 | ### Why on-demand rather than event-driven?
33 | 
34 | 1. **Demo constraint** — the demo is a ≤3-minute video. A background daemon adds
35 |    setup complexity (GitLab webhook configuration, a running process outside Bob)
36 |    with no visible payoff inside the video window.
37 | 2. **Trust** — for a first-exposure demo, showing the user explicitly triggering
38 |    an agent and seeing it respond builds more trust than having changes appear
39 |    "automatically."
40 | 3. **No extra infrastructure** — stdio-transport MCP + Docker is the only runtime
41 |    dependency. An event loop would require a webhook receiver service.
42 | 
43 | ### How a post-MVP event-driven model would work
44 | 
45 | When the demo is proven, the natural upgrade path is:
46 | 
47 | 1. Register a GitLab system hook (or project webhook) pointing at a lightweight
48 |    listener process (e.g. a small Express server in `gitlab-local/`).
49 | 2. The listener receives `issue` / `merge_request` events and writes them to a
50 |    queue file or calls the MCP server directly.
51 | 3. A scheduled Bob shell session (cron or systemd timer) drains the queue,
52 |    runs the relevant agent(s) programmatically, and posts results as GitLab
53 |    comments — without requiring the developer to be in Bob at all.
54 | 
55 | This path is **not built for the demo** and is listed here only as design intent.
56 | 
57 | ---
58 | 
59 | ## Execution model within a Bob session
60 | 
61 | When the user triggers a governance action (e.g. "run a full audit"), Bob
62 | executes the agents **sequentially by default**, collecting all findings before
63 | presenting them:
64 | 
65 | ```
66 | User: "audit the backlog"
67 | Bob:
68 |   1. Fetch all open issues via gitlab-local MCP (read, alwaysAllow)
69 |   2. Run AC agent   → findings[]
70 |   3. Run AM agent   → findings[]
71 |   4. Run DEP agent  → findings[]
72 |   5. Run ST agent   → findings[]
73 |   6. Present unified review interface (see "Human review interface" below)
74 | ```
75 | 
76 | For a **single-issue drill-down** (e.g. "check issue #7"), only the agents
77 | relevant to that issue run.
78 | 
79 | For **long-context tasks** (dependency graph across 50+ issues), Bob may use
80 | `spawn_subagent` to run DEP in parallel with AC+AM, merging results before
81 | the review step. The skill's `SKILL.md` governs when subagents are spawned.
82 | 
83 | ### P1 — test-coverage agent slot
84 | 
85 | TC slots in after ST in the sequential pipeline. It is disabled by default
86 | (the seed data does not include test files for the MVP). To enable:
87 | 
88 | 1. Populate `weather-app/` with at least one test file (e.g. `weather.test.js`).
89 | 2. Configure the TC agent's scan path in `.sdlc-harness.json`:
90 |    `"testGlob": "weather-app/**/*.test.*"`.
91 | 3. The skill will include TC in subsequent audit runs automatically.
92 | 
93 | ---
94 | 
95 | ## Context sharing
96 | 
97 | All agents in a single audit run share one context object assembled at the
98 | start of the run:
99 | 
100 | ```jsonc
101 | {
102 |   "project": { "url": "…", "name": "…" },          // from .sdlc-harness.json
103 |   "workflowStates": ["Open", "In Progress", "Done"], // from .sdlc-harness.json
104 |   "transitionRules": { … },                          // from .sdlc-harness.json
105 |   "issues": [ … ],                                   // fetched once via MCP
106 |   "mergeRequests": [ … ]                             // fetched once via MCP
107 | }
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | **Issues and MRs are fetched exactly once** per audit run and passed to every
111 | agent. This avoids redundant API calls and ensures all agents reason over the
112 | same snapshot (no TOCTOU skew between agents).
113 | 
114 | The shared context is assembled in Bob's working memory for the session; it is
115 | not persisted to disk beyond the `.sdlc-harness.json` config file.
116 | 
117 | ---
118 | 
119 | ## Human review interface
120 | 
121 | After all agents have run, Bob presents findings in a **single unified review
122 | loop** rather than agent-by-agent prompts. This keeps the developer in one
123 | mental frame (reviewing suggestions) rather than switching between four separate
124 | agent conversations.
125 | 
126 | ### Presentation format (per finding)
127 | 
128 | ```
129 | ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
130 | [AC] Issue #12 — "Add weather forecast widget"
131 |   ⚠  No acceptance criteria found.
132 | 
133 |   Suggested AC:
134 |     Given the user is on the dashboard
135 |     When they view the forecast panel
136 |     Then they see a 5-day temperature and precipitation summary
137 | 
138 |   → apply / edit / skip / reject
139 | ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
140 | ```
141 | 
142 | ### User responses
143 | 
144 | | Response | Interpretation | Action |
145 | |---|---|---|
146 | | "apply" / "yes" / "accept" | Approved as-is | Write to GitLab; log outcome = "accepted" |
147 | | "edit: <new text>" | Approved with changes | Write edited version; log outcome = "edited", editedFields noted |
148 | | "skip" | Deferred | No write; not logged (neutral, try again next run) |
149 | | "reject" / "no" / "dismiss" | Explicitly rejected | No write; log outcome = "rejected" |
150 | 
151 | Bob does not proceed to the next finding until the user has responded. A vague
152 | "ok" counts as "apply."
153 | 
154 | ### Conflict resolution
155 | 
156 | A **conflict** arises when two agents produce suggestions that contradict each
157 | other on the same issue — most commonly:
158 | 
159 | - DEP suggests issue A *blocks* issue B (implying A must be done first),
160 |   while ST suggests transitioning A to "Done" (implying A is already complete).
161 | - AM rewrites a description in a way that would invalidate existing AC drafted
162 |   by AC in the same run.
163 | 
164 | **Detection:** Bob checks for overlapping `issueIid` values across agent finding
165 | sets before presenting the review. If a conflict is found, the affected findings
166 | are grouped together and flagged:
167 | 
168 | ```
169 | ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
170 | ⚡ CONFLICT — Issue #7 has suggestions from two agents that may contradict:
171 | 
172 |   [ST] Proposed transition: Open → In Progress
173 |        (reason: MR !3 referencing this issue was opened 2h ago)
174 | 
175 |   [DEP] Proposed link: #7 blocks #9
176 |        (reason: both issues describe the same auth token refresh logic)
177 | 
178 |   Review both before applying either. Applying ST first is recommended
179 |   if the work is genuinely in progress; applying DEP first is recommended
180 |   if #7 is a blocker that should not move until #9 is acknowledged.
181 | 
182 |   → apply ST first / apply DEP first / apply both / skip both
183 | ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
184 | ```
185 | 
186 | The user decides the order or skips both. Bob does not auto-resolve conflicts.
187 | 
188 | ---
189 | 
190 | ## Telemetry
191 | 
192 | Every apply / edit / reject outcome is appended to `sdlc-harness-telemetry.jsonl`
193 | in the repo root (one JSON object per line, never overwritten — append-only):
194 | 
195 | ```jsonc
196 | {
197 |   "ts": "2025-09-01T14:32:10Z",
198 |   "agent": "AC",
199 |   "issueIid": 12,
200 |   "action": "draft_ac",
201 |   "outcome": "accepted",   // "accepted" | "edited" | "rejected"
202 |   "editedFields": []       // populated when outcome = "edited"
203 | }
204 | ```
205 | 
206 | The acceptance rate (accepted / (accepted + rejected)) is the primary trust
207 | metric cited in the demo. `sdlc-harness-telemetry.jsonl` is gitignored; it
208 | does not contain issue content, only metadata.

1 | #!/usr/bin/env bash
2 | # smoke.sh — Validates that the full stack is healthy after `docker compose up`.
3 | # Exits 0 only if both services return the expected HTTP responses.
4 | # Run from any directory — it resolves its own path.
5 | set -euo pipefail
6 | 
7 | GITLAB_URL="http://localhost:8080"
8 | DEMO_SITE_URL="http://localhost:8081"
9 | 
10 | # How long (seconds) to wait for each service before giving up
11 | TIMEOUT=300
12 | INTERVAL=5
13 | 
14 | pass() { echo "  ✓  $1"; }
15 | fail() { echo "  ✗  $1"; exit 1; }
16 | 
17 | wait_for() {
18 |   local name="$1"
19 |   local url="$2"
20 |   local deadline=$(( $(date +%s) + TIMEOUT ))
21 | 
22 |   echo "Waiting for $name ($url)..."
23 |   while true; do
24 |     local code
25 |     code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 5 "$url" 2>/dev/null || echo "000")
26 |     if [ "$code" = "200" ] || [ "$code" = "302" ]; then
27 |       pass "$name returned HTTP $code"
28 |       return 0
29 |     fi
30 |     if [ "$(date +%s)" -ge "$deadline" ]; then
31 |       fail "$name did not become healthy within ${TIMEOUT}s (last HTTP code: $code)"
32 |     fi
33 |     echo "    HTTP $code — retrying in ${INTERVAL}s..."
34 |     sleep "$INTERVAL"
35 |   done
36 | }

40 | echo " SDLC Harness — stack smoke test"

42 | echo ""

46 |

Here's the full sequence to get it running:

**Step 1 — First-time only: create your `.env` file**
```bash
cd gitlab-local
cp .env.example .env
# then edit .env and set GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD to something strong
```

**Step 2 — Start the stack** *(first boot takes 3–5 min)*
```bash
docker compose up -d
```

**Step 3 — Wait for GitLab to be healthy**
```bash
./smoke.sh
```
Polls until both services respond. When it prints `All checks passed`, continue.

**Step 4 — Seed demo users, group, and project** *(run once)*
```bash
./manage.sh seed
```

**Step 5 — Open in browser**
- GitLab UI: **http://localhost:8080** — login as `root` with your password
- Demo weather app: **http://localhost:8081**
- Demo project: **http://localhost:8080/sdlc-harness/weather-dashboard**

---

**Day-to-day commands (already running):**
```bash
./manage.sh start    # start
./manage.sh stop     # stop
./manage.sh status   # check health
./manage.sh logs     # tail logs
```

**Full reset (clean demo slate):**
```bash
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d
./manage.sh seed
```

> ⚠️ **Windows note:** `smoke.sh` and `manage.sh` are bash scripts — run them in Git Bash, WSL, or prefix with `bash smoke.sh` / `bash manage.sh seed`.

# MCP Tool Registration Issue

## Summary

The MCP server builds and its smoke tests pass, but all four registered tools fail when invoked through the real MCP stdio transport.

## Root Cause

In `mcp-server/src/index.ts`, tools are registered using:

```typescript
tool.argsSchema.shape ?? {}
```

Each tool uses a Zod discriminated-union schema. These schemas do not expose a `shape` property, so the fallback `{}` is used. The MCP server consequently publishes every tool with an empty input schema and removes supplied arguments before execution.

The tool then attempts to parse the empty object and fails because the required `action` discriminator is missing.

## Observed Result

The server publishes the following tools with no input properties:

- `gitlab-issue-reader`
- `gitlab-issue-writer`
- `gitlab-mr-reader-writer`
- `work-item-format`

Calling any of them returns an `invalid_union_discriminator` error for `action`.

## Why Existing Tests Pass

`mcp-server/src/smoke.ts` imports each tool implementation and calls its `execute()` function directly. It does not start the MCP server or invoke tools through stdio.

Therefore:

- `npm run build` passes.
- `npm run smoke` reports 23 passing checks.
- Real MCP tool calls still fail.

## Tasks Affected

| Task | Impact |
|---|---|
| 7 | Scaffold is present and not the direct cause. |
| 8 | GitLab client works independently. |
| 9 | Environment loading works independently. |
| 10 | Root cause: incorrect MCP schema registration. |
| 11 | Issue tools cannot be used through MCP. |
| 12 | Merge-request tools cannot be used through MCP. |
| 13 | Work-item formatting tool cannot be used through MCP. |
| 14 | Separate Bob configuration inconsistencies remain. |
| 15 | Installer cannot deliver a functioning MCP setup until Task 10 is fixed. |
| 16 | Validation is a false positive because it bypasses the MCP transport. |

Tasks 17 and later also depend on these tools, so the agents cannot operate end-to-end until this issue is resolved.

## Required Resolution

1. Register each complete Zod input schema with the MCP SDK instead of reading `.shape` from a discriminated union.
2. Add an integration test that starts `dist/index.js` through `StdioClientTransport`.
3. Verify that `listTools()` publishes the expected `action` and action-specific fields.
4. Invoke every registered tool through MCP and fail the smoke test if any invocation produces a schema error.
5. Re-run the documented Task 16 gate.

## Completion Criteria

The issue is resolved when:

- `npm install`, `npm run build`, and `npm run smoke` pass.
- All registered tools expose non-empty input schemas.
- Valid MCP calls reach their implementations without an `action` validation error.
- Invalid calls return intentional validation errors.
- The live GitLab checks pass when the local GitLab stack and credentials are available.

So `registerTool` with the discriminated union schema is still producing `{}`. The issue is that `normalizeObjectSchema` in the SDK (line 114-156) checks for `.shape` on a v3 schema and `.shape` on a discriminated union is `undefined` — so it returns `undefined` and the empty schema is used for `listTools`. But `validateToolInput` correctly falls back to parsing with the raw schema.

This means the SDK's `normalizeObjectSchema` does not handle discriminated unions for schema publication. The correct approach for discriminated unions is to convert them to JSON Schema manually and use the lower-level `Server` API (not `McpServer`), OR wrap the discriminated union in a way the SDK can inspect.

The real fix: use `zodToJsonSchema` directly on the discriminated union and register using the low-level `Server.setRequestHandler`. Let me check how to do this cleanly:

`zodToJsonSchema` produces a proper `anyOf` schema for discriminated unions — not `properties`. The SDK's `normalizeObjectSchema` doesn't handle this case (it only handles plain `z.object()`), which is why `listTools` always returns `{}`.

The correct solution: bypass `McpServer.registerTool` for publishing the schema, and instead use the lower-level `server.server.setRequestHandler` directly. But that's complex. The cleaner approach that works within the SDK's design is to **manually convert the discriminated union to a JSON Schema and register tools using the low-level `Server` API** with `ListToolsRequestSchema` and `CallToolRequestSchema`.

data.content:
The MCP protocol requires `type: "object"` at the top level. The cleanest approach that satisfies the protocol constraint is to build a **helper function** in `index.ts` that flattens a discriminated union into a single `type: "object"` schema with `anyOf` inside `properties` — but actually the right approach, used by all real MCP tool servers with discriminated unions, is to **wrap the `anyOf` inside an object**:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": { ... merged union of all properties ... },
  "required": ["action"]
}
```

I'll write a `flattenDiscriminatedUnion` helper that extracts all properties from all variants and builds a proper object schema:

Fixed and committed. Here's the full summary:

---

## What was wrong

In [`src/index.ts`](mcp-server/src/index.ts:45), `server.tool()` was passed `tool.argsSchema.shape ?? {}`. Discriminated unions have no `.shape` property — the fallback `{}` meant every tool was published with an empty input schema. Real MCP calls from Bob would receive no argument guidance and fail immediately with `invalid_union_discriminator`.

The existing smoke tests passed because they called `tool.execute()` directly, bypassing the MCP transport entirely.

## What was fixed

1. **[`src/index.ts`](mcp-server/src/index.ts)** — Replaced `McpServer` with the low-level `Server` API. Added a `buildInputSchema()` helper that flattens each discriminated union into a valid `type: "object"` schema (required by the MCP protocol spec), with the `action` discriminator as an `enum` and all per-variant fields merged as optional properties.

2. **[`src/smoke.ts`](mcp-server/src/smoke.ts)** — Added `testMcpTransportIntegration()` which spawns `dist/index.js` as a real subprocess via `StdioClientTransport`, calls `listTools`, verifies all 4 tools publish non-empty schemas, and invokes `work-item-format` through the actual stdio transport.

177 | // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
178 | // Validation helper
179 | // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
180 | 
181 | interface ValidationViolation {
182 |   field: "title" | "description" | "acceptanceCriteria";
183 |   rule: string;
184 |   suggestion?: string;
185 | }
186 | 
187 | function validateItem(
188 |   type: WorkItemType,
189 |   title: string,
190 |   description?: string,
191 |   acceptanceCriteria?: string
192 | ): ValidationViolation[] {
193 |   const template = TEMPLATES[type];
194 |   const violations: ValidationViolation[] = [];
195 | 
196 |   // --- Title checks ---
197 |   if (title.length > 120) {
198 |     violations.push({
199 |       field: "title",
200 |       rule: "Title exceeds 120 characters.",
201 |       suggestion: "Shorten to the core action/outcome.",
202 |     });
203 |   }
204 |   if (type === "User Story" && !title.toLowerCase().startsWith("as a")) {
205 |     violations.push({
206 |       field: "title",
207 |       rule: "User Story titles must follow Connextra format: 'As a <role>, I can...'.",
208 |       suggestion: `Rewrite as: "${template.example.title}"`,
209 |     });
210 |   }
211 |   if (type === "Bug" && !title.includes(":")) {
212 |     violations.push({
213 |       field: "title",
214 |       rule: "Bug titles must follow '<Component>: <symptom>' format.",
215 |       suggestion: `Example: "${template.example.title}"`,
216 |     });
217 |   }
218 | 
219 |   // --- Description checks ---
220 |   if (!description || description.trim().length === 0) {
221 |     violations.push({
222 |       field: "description",
223 |       rule: "Description is empty.",
224 |       suggestion: `Use the ${type} template:\n${template.descriptionStructure}`,
225 |     });
226 |   }
227 | 
228 |   // --- Acceptance criteria checks (User Story and Bug only) ---
229 |   if (type === "User Story" || type === "Bug") {
230 |     if (!acceptanceCriteria || acceptanceCriteria.trim().length === 0) {
231 |       violations.push({
232 |         field: "acceptanceCriteria",
233 |         rule: "Acceptance criteria are required for User Stories and Bugs.",
234 |         suggestion: `Use Given-When-Then format:\n${template.acceptanceCriteriaFormat}`,
235 |       });
236 |     } else {
237 |       const hasGiven = /given/i.test(acceptanceCriteria);
238 |       const hasWhen = /when/i.test(acceptanceCriteria);
239 |       const hasThen = /then/i.test(acceptanceCriteria);
240 |       if (!hasGiven || !hasWhen || !hasThen) {
241 |         violations.push({
242 |           field: "acceptanceCriteria",
243 |           rule: "Acceptance criteria must use Given-When-Then structure.",
244 |           suggestion: `Example:\n${template.acceptanceCriteriaFormat}`,
245 |         });
246 |       }
247 |     }
248 |   }
249 | 
250 |   return violations;
251 | }

Build a complete, minimal demo web application for our IBM hackathon project, “SDLC Harness.”

  - Weather condition
  - Humidity
  - Wind speed

```

# Weather Dashboard — SDLC Harness Demo

A minimal, self-contained web application built to demonstrate an end-to-end SDLC
workflow using the **SDLC Harness** project.  The app itself is intentionally simple
so that every team member can understand the full codebase in minutes, then use it
to practise branching, committing, reviewing, and tracing changes back to work items.

---

## Purpose

This application serves as the **demo artefact** for the SDLC Harness IBM Hackathon
project.  It is not a production weather service; it uses deterministic mock data so
that the same city name always produces the same result, making demo walkthroughs
repeatable without an API key or network connection.

---

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Application shell — semantic HTML, accessible landmarks and form |
| `styles.css` | All styling — CSS custom properties, card layout, dark mode, responsive breakpoints |
| `app.js` | All runtime behaviour — mock data, search, validation, loading state, theme toggle |
| `README.md` | This file |
| `tests.md` | Manual test checklist |

---

## Running Locally

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Open **`index.html`** directly in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
   No server, build step, or package manager is required.

```
# macOS / Linux (optional)
open index.html

# Windows (optional)
start index.html
```

---

## Features

- **City search** — Enter any city name and click Search (or press Enter) to see mock
  weather data generated deterministically from the city name.
- **Default result** — "New York" is displayed on first load so the page is never blank.
- **Validation** — An error message is shown when the city field is empty.
- **Loading state** — A brief spinner simulates an async data fetch (300 ms).
- **Light / Dark theme** — Toggle button in the header; selection is persisted in
  `localStorage` across page reloads.
- **Accessible** — Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and visible focus
  indicators throughout.
- **Responsive** — Single-column layout on mobile (≤ 600 px), side-by-side header on
  wider screens.

---

## Suggested SDLC Demo Changes

Use these as concrete tasks to walk through branching, committing, reviewing, and
linking changes back to work items in SDLC Harness:

1. **Add a 5-day forecast section** — extend `getMockWeather()` in `app.js` to return
   an array of daily forecasts and add a new card row in `index.html`.

2. **Change temperature units** — add a °C / °F toggle; store the preference in
   `localStorage` alongside the theme.

3. **Stricter city-name validation** — reject inputs that contain numbers or special
   characters; add the regex rule to `handleSearch()` and expand the test checklist.

4. **Write automated unit tests** — create `tests.js` using plain `console.assert`
   calls (no test framework needed) and open it in the browser console to verify
   `getMockWeather()` and `hashString()` behave correctly.

5. **Real API integration** — replace `getMockWeather()` with a `fetch()` call to the
   [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key required) and handle the
   async response; update `tests.md` to cover network-error states.

6. **Internationalisation** — add a language selector that switches UI strings between
   English and another language using a simple JavaScript object map.

# Manual Test Checklist — Weather Dashboard

Use this checklist to verify the application before merging any branch.
Open `index.html` directly in a browser; no server is required.

Mark each item **✅ Pass**, **❌ Fail**, or **⚠ N/A** when testing.

---

## 1. Default Weather Display

| # | Step | Expected Result | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | Open `index.html` in a browser | Page loads without errors (check browser console) | |
| 1.2 | Observe the weather card without interacting | Card shows "New York" with temperature, condition, humidity, wind speed, and a "Last updated" time | |
| 1.3 | No city is entered in the input field | Input field is empty; no validation message is shown | |

---

## 2. Valid City Search

| # | Step | Expected Result | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Type `London` into the city input and click **Search** | Weather card updates to show "London" with deterministic mock data | |
| 2.2 | Search for `London` a second time | Identical temperature, condition, humidity, and wind speed as the first search (deterministic) | |
| 2.3 | Search for a different city, e.g. `Tokyo` | Card updates to show "Tokyo" with different values from "London" | |
| 2.4 | Search for a multi-word city, e.g. `Los Angeles` | Card displays "Los Angeles" in title case | |
| 2.5 | Search for a city name with mixed case, e.g. `pARIS` | Card displays "Paris" (title-cased) | |

---

## 3. Empty City Validation

+# Weather Dashboard — SDLC Harness Demo
+
+A minimal, self-contained web application built to demonstrate an end-to-end SDLC
+workflow using the **SDLC Harness** project.  The app itself is intentionally simple
+so that every team member can understand the full codebase in minutes, then use it
+to practise branching, committing, reviewing, and tracing changes back to work items.
+
+---
+
+## Purpose
+
+This application serves as the **demo artefact** for the SDLC Harness IBM Hackathon
+project.  It is not a production weather service; it uses deterministic mock data so
+that the same city name always produces the same result, making demo walkthroughs
+repeatable without an API key or network connection.
+
+---
+
+## Files
+
+| File | Description |
+|---|---|
+| `index.html` | Application shell — semantic HTML, accessible landmarks and form |
+| `styles.css` | All styling — CSS custom properties, card layout, dark mode, responsive breakpoints |
+| `app.js` | All runtime behaviour — mock data, search, validation, loading state, theme toggle |
+| `README.md` | This file |
+| `tests.md` | Manual test checklist |
+
+---
+
+## Running Locally
+
+1. Clone or download this repository.
+2. Open **`index.html`** directly in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
+   No server, build step, or package manager is required.
+
+```
+# macOS / Linux (optional)
+open index.html
+
+# Windows (optional)
+start index.html
+```
+
+---
+
+## Features
+
+- **City search** — Enter any city name and click Search (or press Enter) to see mock
+  weather data generated deterministically from the city name.
+- **Default result** — "New York" is displayed on first load so the page is never blank.
+- **Validation** — An error message is shown when the city field is empty.
+- **Loading state** — A brief spinner simulates an async data fetch (300 ms).
+- **Light / Dark theme** — Toggle button in the header; selection is persisted in
+  `localStorage` across page reloads.
+- **Accessible** — Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and visible focus
+  indicators throughout.
+- **Responsive** — Single-column layout on mobile (≤ 600 px), side-by-side header on
+  wider screens.
+
+---
+
+## Suggested SDLC Demo Changes
+
+Use these as concrete tasks to walk through branching, committing, reviewing, and
+linking changes back to work items in SDLC Harness:
+
+1. **Add a 5-day forecast section** — extend `getMockWeather()` in `app.js` to return
+   an array of daily forecasts and add a new card row in `index.html`.
+
+2. **Change temperature units** — add a °C / °F toggle; store the preference in
+   `localStorage` alongside the theme.
+
+3. **Stricter city-name validation** — reject inputs that contain numbers or special
+   characters; add the regex rule to `handleSearch()` and expand the test checklist.
+
+4. **Write automated unit tests** — create `tests.js` using plain `console.assert`
+   calls (no test framework needed) and open it in the browser console to verify
+   `getMockWeather()` and `hashString()` behave correctly.
+
+5. **Real API integration** — replace `getMockWeather()` with a `fetch()` call to the
+   [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key required) and handle the
+   async response; update `tests.md` to cover network-error states.
+
+6. **Internationalisation** — add a language selector that switches UI strings between
+   English and another language using a simple JavaScript object map.

## Files Created

| File | Lines | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| [`index.html`](index.html) | 97 | Semantic HTML shell — skip link, sticky header, search form with ARIA, weather card with `<dl>` details, loading overlay |
| [`styles.css`](styles.css) | 320 | Full CSS — 30+ design tokens via custom properties, card layout, dark-mode override block, CSS spinner, responsive breakpoint |
| [`app.js`](app.js) | 215 | All runtime JS — hash-based mock data, form validation, 300 ms loading simulation, card rendering, theme toggle with localStorage |
| [`README.md`](README.md) | 88 | Purpose, file table, one-step local run instructions, 6 suggested SDLC demo changes |
| [`tests.md`](tests.md) | 110 | 8-section manual checklist covering all functional and accessibility requirements |

---

## Implemented Functionality

**Mock data** — [`hashString()`](app.js:38) derives a stable integer from the city name, which seeds temperature (20–100 °F), condition (9 options), humidity, and wind speed — so the same city always returns identical values across page reloads.

**Search & validation** — [`handleSearch()`](app.js:148) validates for an empty field, shows a red inline error with ARIA `role="alert"`, and clears it as soon as the user types again.

**Loading state** — A CSS spinner overlay covers the card for 300 ms after Search is clicked; the button is disabled during that window to prevent duplicate triggers.

**Enter-key support** — Handled natively via `<form>` submit; no extra key listener needed.

**Theme toggle** — [`applyTheme()`](app.js:188) sets `data-theme` on `<body>`, updates `aria-label`, and persists the choice to `localStorage` under `sdlc-theme`. On load, the saved preference is restored before first paint.

**Accessibility** — Visible `:focus-visible` outlines, skip link, `aria-required`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-live="polite"` on validation and loading regions, and semantic landmarks throughout.

**Responsive** — Below 600 px the search form stacks vertically, the detail grid collapses to one column, and the header wraps cleanly.

## Where We Are

### What was done

The **SDLC Harness** IBM Hackathon project needed a concrete, traceable demo application — something real enough to show an end-to-end software development lifecycle, but simple enough that every team member can read the entire codebase in minutes.

A **Weather Dashboard** web app was built to serve that role. It lives in `<WORKSPACE>` as three plain files:

- [`index.html`](index.html) — the page structure
- [`styles.css`](styles.css) — all visual design
- [`app.js`](app.js) — all behaviour

### Why this approach

| Decision | Reason |
|---|---|
| No framework, no build step | Anyone on the team can open `index.html` and it just works — zero setup friction for a hackathon |
| Deterministic mock data (hash-based) | No API key needed; same city always returns same data, so demo walkthroughs are repeatable |
| CSS custom properties for theming | Dark mode is a single override block — easy to understand and easy to change |
| Semantic HTML + ARIA | Demonstrates accessibility practices as part of the SDLC, not an afterthought |
| Separated HTML / CSS / JS | Each file is a clean, reviewable unit — ideal for showing a focused PR diff per change |

The app is intentionally minimal so that **the SDLC workflow around it** (branches, commits, reviews, work items) is the real demo — not the app itself.

---

## What's Next

The app is ready to be the artefact for your SDLC Harness demo. The typical next steps, roughly in order:

### 1. Connect it to your GitLab workflow
- Create a GitLab issue (User Story or Feature) for the initial app creation
- Commit the current files on a branch, open an MR, review, and merge — this becomes the first traced change in your SDLC demo

### 2. Demo a change end-to-end
Pick one small, visible change from [`README.md`](README.md#suggested-sdlc-demo-changes) and walk it through the full cycle:
- Create a work item
- Branch off `main`
- Make the code change
- Open an MR linked to the work item
- Review and merge

Good first candidates (all small and isolated):
- **°C / °F unit toggle** — one new button, a few lines of JS
- **Stricter city validation** — one regex check in [`handleSearch()`](app.js:148)
- **5-day forecast row** — extend [`getMockWeather()`](app.js:53) and add a new HTML section

### 3. Add automated unit tests
Create a `tests.js` file using plain `console.assert` — no framework needed. Tests for [`hashString()`](app.js:38) and [`getMockWeather()`](app.js:53) are the obvious starting point. This demonstrates the "test" phase of the SDLC.

### 4. Demonstrate a bug fix
Intentionally introduce a small bug on a branch (e.g. the validation not triggering on whitespace-only input), file it as a Bug work item, fix it, and trace the fix back through the MR to the item.

### 5. (Stretch) Real API integration
Replace [`getMockWeather()`](app.js:53) with a `fetch()` call to the [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) — free, no key required. This shows the "external dependency" phase of the lifecycle.

---

The foundation is solid. The next move is step 1 — get it into GitLab and start tracing changes.

data.content:
**Hard refresh the page now** (`Ctrl+Shift+R` or `Ctrl+F5`).

---

### What was wrong and why

The root cause was a **CSS specificity conflict** between the browser's built-in `hidden` attribute style and the stylesheet rule:

- The HTML `hidden` attribute tells the browser `display: none`
- The CSS rule `.loading-overlay { display: flex }` has higher specificity than the browser's built-in stylesheet, so it **won over `hidden`** — the overlay was always visible

The fix moves `display: flex` into a `.loading-overlay:not([hidden])` selector, so it only applies when the element is actually visible. When `hidden` is present, no `display` rule fires at all, and the browser's default `display: none` from `hidden` takes effect correctly.

After the hard refresh: the card loads with New York data, the spinner is gone, and it will only appear briefly (300 ms) when you click Search.

## What Has Been Done

### The Project
A complete demo web application called **Weather Dashboard** was built from scratch for the **SDLC Harness** IBM Hackathon project. It lives at `<WORKSPACE>` and opens directly by double-clicking [`index.html`](index.html).

---

### Files Created

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`index.html`](index.html) | Page structure — header, search form, weather card, footer |
| [`styles.css`](styles.css) | All visual design — colours, layout, dark mode, responsive |
| [`app.js`](app.js) | All behaviour — search, mock data, validation, theme toggle |
| [`README.md`](README.md) | Purpose, run instructions, suggested SDLC demo changes |
| [`tests.md`](tests.md) | Manual test checklist for the whole app |

---

### What the App Does

- **Loads with default data** — New York weather card shown immediately on open
- **City search** — type any city, press Enter or click Search → mock weather data appears
- **Deterministic mock data** — same city always returns same values (no API needed); derived from a hash of the city name
- **Validation** — red inline error if you search with an empty field
- **Loading spinner** — brief 300 ms spinner overlay when Search is clicked
- **Dark / light theme** — toggle in the header; choice saved in `localStorage` and restored on reload
- **Responsive** — works on desktop and mobile
- **Accessible** — keyboard navigation, ARIA labels, visible focus outlines, screen-reader announcements

---

### Bugs Fixed

Two bugs were found and fixed after the initial build:

1. **Redundant `setLoading()` logic** in [`app.js`](app.js:131) — a double-write meant the overlay state was unreliable
2. **CSS overriding HTML `hidden` attribute** in [`styles.css`](styles.css:275) — `display: flex` on `.loading-overlay` was beating the browser's built-in `hidden` rule, causing the spinner to show permanently even when it should be hidden. Fixed by moving `display: flex` into a `.loading-overlay:not([hidden])` selector so it only activates when the overlay is actually visible

---

### Current State

The app is **working correctly**:
- ✅ Opens in a browser with no server or install
- ✅ Default New York card on load
- ✅ Search works, spinner appears and disappears correctly
- ✅ Validation, dark mode, and theme persistence all work
- ✅ No JavaScript errors

---

### What's Next

The app is ready to be used as the demo artefact for SDLC Harness. Typical next steps:

1. **Connect to GitLab** — commit to a branch, open an MR, merge, and trace it to a work item
2. **Demo a tracked change** — pick one small change (e.g. °C/°F toggle, stricter validation) and walk it through the full branch → commit → review → merge cycle
3. **Add automated tests** — a plain `tests.js` using `console.assert` to verify the mock data functions
4. **Stretch: real API** — replace mock data with a free `fetch()` call to Open-Meteo (no key required)

arguments.html:
Session Summary IBM Hackathon

Project: SDLC Harness  ·  Demo Application: Weather Dashboard  ·  Location:

Objective

Build a minimal, self-contained demo web application to serve as the traceable artefact for the SDLC Harness project — something real enough to demonstrate a full software development lifecycle (branches, commits, reviews, work items) but simple enough for any team member to read and change in minutes. No backend, no framework, no build step.

Files Created

FilePurpose
index.htmlPage shell — semantic HTML, sticky header, search form, weather card, footer
styles.cssAll styling — CSS custom property tokens, card layout, dark mode override block, responsive breakpoint
app.jsAll runtime behaviour — hash-based mock data, validation, loading state, card rendering, theme persistence
README.mdPurpose, file listing, one-step local run instructions, 6 suggested SDLC demo changes
tests.mdManual test checklist — 8 sections, 35+ test cases covering all features and accessibility

Implemented Features

Default weather card New York data shown on first load — page is never blank
City search Type any city, press Enter or click Search — deterministic mock data returned
Mock data engine Hash of city name seeds temperature, condition, humidity, wind — same city always = same result
Input validation Red inline error + ARIA alert when field is empty; clears on next keystroke
Loading state 300 ms spinner overlay; Search button disabled during load to prevent duplicates
Dark / light theme toggle Header button switches theme; choice persisted in localStorage across reloads
Responsive layout Stacks vertically on mobile (≤ 600 px); works on all screen sizes
Accessibility Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, skip link, visible focus outlines, live regions

Bugs Found & Fixed

Bug 1 — Redundant setLoading() logic (app.js)
The loading function set hidden twice in conflicting ways, making the overlay state unreliable. Simplified to a single clean assignment.
Bug 2 — CSS display:flex overriding HTML hidden attribute (styles.css)
The .loading-overlay { display: flex } rule had higher specificity than the browser's built-in hidden style, so the spinner was permanently visible even when it should be hidden. Fixed by moving display: flex into .loading-overlay:not([hidden]) so it only fires when the element is actually shown.

Current Status

✓ Opens in browser — no install needed ✓ Default New York card on load ✓ Search & spinner work correctly ✓ Validation working ✓ Dark mode & persistence working ✓ No JavaScript errors ✓ Responsive on mobile

Recommended Next Steps

  • 1
    Connect to GitLab Commit the current files on a branch, open an MR, and merge — this becomes the first fully-traced change in your SDLC demo
  • 2
    Demo a tracked change end-to-end Pick one small change (°C/°F toggle, stricter validation, forecast row), create a work item, branch, commit, review, and merge it
  • 3
    Add automated unit tests Create tests.js using plain console.assert — verify hashString() and getMockWeather() with no test framework needed
  • 4
    Demo a bug fix cycle Intentionally introduce a small bug (e.g. whitespace-only input bypassing validation), file it as a Bug work item, fix it, trace it back through the MR
  • 5
    Stretch: real API integration Replace getMockWeather() with a fetch() to Open-Meteo (free, no key required) to show the external-dependency phase of the lifecycle

# Weather Dashboard — SDLC Harness Demo

A minimal, self-contained web application built to demonstrate an end-to-end SDLC
workflow using the **SDLC Harness** project.  The app itself is intentionally simple
so that every team member can understand the full codebase in minutes, then use it
to practise branching, committing, reviewing, and tracing changes back to work items.

---

## Purpose

This application serves as the **demo artefact** for the SDLC Harness IBM Hackathon
project.  It is not a production weather service; it uses deterministic mock data so
that the same city name always produces the same result, making demo walkthroughs
repeatable without an API key or network connection.

---

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Application shell — semantic HTML, accessible landmarks and form |
| `styles.css` | All styling — CSS custom properties, card layout, dark mode, responsive breakpoints |
| `app.js` | All runtime behaviour — mock data, search, validation, loading state, theme toggle |
| `README.md` | This file |
| `tests.md` | Manual test checklist |

---

## Running Locally

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Open **`index.html`** directly in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
   No server, build step, or package manager is required.

```
# macOS / Linux (optional)
open index.html

# Windows (optional)
start index.html
```

---

## Features

- **City search** — Enter any city name and click Search (or press Enter) to see mock
  weather data generated deterministically from the city name.
- **Default result** — "New York" is displayed on first load so the page is never blank.
- **Validation** — An error message is shown when the city field is empty.
- **Loading state** — A brief spinner simulates an async data fetch (300 ms).
- **Light / Dark theme** — Toggle button in the header; selection is persisted in
  `localStorage` across page reloads.
- **Accessible** — Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and visible focus
  indicators throughout.
- **Responsive** — Single-column layout on mobile (≤ 600 px), side-by-side header on
  wider screens.

---

## Suggested SDLC Demo Changes

Use these as concrete tasks to walk through branching, committing, reviewing, and
linking changes back to work items in SDLC Harness:

1. **Add a 5-day forecast section** — extend `getMockWeather()` in `app.js` to return
   an array of daily forecasts and add a new card row in `index.html`.

2. **Change temperature units** — add a °C / °F toggle; store the preference in
   `localStorage` alongside the theme.

3. **Stricter city-name validation** — reject inputs that contain numbers or special
   characters; add the regex rule to `handleSearch()` and expand the test checklist.

4. **Write automated unit tests** — create `tests.js` using plain `console.assert`
   calls (no test framework needed) and open it in the browser console to verify
   `getMockWeather()` and `hashString()` behave correctly.

5. **Real API integration** — replace `getMockWeather()` with a `fetch()` call to the
   [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key required) and handle the
   async response; update `tests.md` to cover network-error states.

6. **Internationalisation** — add a language selector that switches UI strings between
   English and another language using a simple JavaScript object map.

# IBM Hackathon GitHub Project Template

This GitHub project template is for IBM Hackathon projects. It includes pre-configured security files to help prevent accidental credential commits and potential account suspension during the hackathon.

## 🚀 Quick Start

1. **Use this template to create your project:**
   - Click "Use this template" button above and select "Create a new repository"
   - Name your repository
   - Click "Create repository"

2. **Clone your new repository:**

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/HACKATHON-ORG/your-repo-name.git
   cd your-repo-name
   ```

3. **Set up environment variables:**

   ```bash
   # Copy the example file
   cp .env.example .env

   # Edit .env with your actual credentials
   # Use your preferred editor (nano, vim, code, etc.)
   nano .env
   ```

4. **Verify .gitignore is working:**

   ```bash
   # This should NOT show .env file
   git status

   # This should confirm .env is ignored
   git check-ignore -v .env
   ```

5. **Start developing!**

## 🔒 Security Features

This template includes:

- **`.gitignore`** - Prevents committing credentials and live session files
- **`.bobignore`** - Prevents AI assistants from logging credentials
- **`.env.example`** - Template for your environment variables

## 📋 Before Every Commit

Always run this checklist:

- [ ] Reviewed `git diff` for sensitive data
- [ ] No hardcoded API keys or passwords
- [ ] `.env` file is NOT in staged changes
- [ ] No files with "credential" or "secret" in name
- [ ] Used environment variables for all credentials

## 🆘 Need Help?

- Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.MD) for detailed guidelines
- Contact hackathon support through mentor channel
- Ask in the hackathon Slack workspace

---

**Remember:** Security is everyone's responsibility. When in doubt, ask for help!

# Weather Dashboard — SDLC Harness Demo

A minimal, self-contained web application built to demonstrate an end-to-end SDLC
workflow using the **SDLC Harness** project.  The app itself is intentionally simple
so that every team member can understand the full codebase in minutes, then use it
to practise branching, committing, reviewing, and tracing changes back to work items.

---

## Purpose

This application serves as the **demo artefact** for the SDLC Harness IBM Hackathon
project.  It is not a production weather service; it uses deterministic mock data so
that the same city name always produces the same result, making demo walkthroughs
repeatable without an API key or network connection.

---

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Application shell — semantic HTML, accessible landmarks and form |
| `styles.css` | All styling — CSS custom properties, card layout, dark mode, responsive breakpoints |
| `app.js` | All runtime behaviour — mock data, search, validation, loading state, theme toggle |
| `WEATHER-DASHBOARD.md` | This file |
| `tests.md` | Manual test checklist |

---

## Running Locally

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Open **`index.html`** directly in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
   No server, build step, or package manager is required.

```
# macOS / Linux (optional)
open index.html

# Windows (optional)
start index.html
```

---

## Features

- **City search** — Enter any city name and press Enter or click Search to see mock
  weather data generated deterministically from the city name.
- **Default result** — "New York" is displayed on first load so the page is never blank.
- **Validation** — An error message is shown when the city field is empty.
- **Loading state** — A brief spinner simulates an async data fetch (300 ms).
- **Light / Dark theme** — Toggle button in the header; selection is persisted in
  `localStorage` across page reloads.
- **Accessible** — Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and visible focus
  indicators throughout.
- **Responsive** — Single-column layout on mobile (≤ 600 px), side-by-side header on
  wider screens.

---

## Suggested SDLC Demo Changes

Use these as concrete tasks to walk through branching, committing, reviewing, and
linking changes back to work items in SDLC Harness:

1. **Add a 5-day forecast section** — extend `getMockWeather()` in `app.js` to return
   an array of daily forecasts and add a new card row in `index.html`.

2. **Change temperature units** — add a °C / °F toggle; store the preference in
   `localStorage` alongside the theme.

3. **Stricter city-name validation** — reject inputs that contain numbers or special
   characters; add the regex rule to `handleSearch()` and expand the test checklist.

4. **Write automated unit tests** — create `tests.js` using plain `console.assert`
   calls (no test framework needed) and open it in the browser console to verify
   `getMockWeather()` and `hashString()` behave correctly.

5. **Real API integration** — replace `getMockWeather()` with a `fetch()` call to the
   [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key required) and handle the
   async response; update `tests.md` to cover network-error states.

6. **Internationalisation** — add a language selector that switches UI strings between
   English and another language using a simple JavaScript object map.

# IBM Hackathon GitHub Project Template

This GitHub project template is for IBM Hackathon projects. It includes pre-configured security files to help prevent accidental credential commits and potential account suspension during the hackathon.

## 🚀 Quick Start

1. **Use this template to create your project:**
   - Click "Use this template" button above and select "Create a new repository"
   - Name your repository
   - Click "Create repository"

2. **Clone your new repository:**

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/HACKATHON-ORG/your-repo-name.git
   cd your-repo-name
   ```

3. **Set up environment variables:**

   ```bash
   # Copy the example file
   cp .env.example .env

   # Edit .env with your actual credentials
   # Use your preferred editor (nano, vim, code, etc.)
   nano .env
   ```

4. **Verify .gitignore is working:**

   ```bash
   # This should NOT show .env file
   git status

   # This should confirm .env is ignored
   git check-ignore -v .env
   ```

5. **Start developing!**

## 🔒 Security Features

This template includes:

- **`.gitignore`** - Prevents committing credentials and live session files
- **`.bobignore`** - Prevents AI assistants from logging credentials
- **`.env.example`** - Template for your environment variables

## 📋 Before Every Commit

Always run this checklist:

- [ ] Reviewed `git diff` for sensitive data
- [ ] No hardcoded API keys or passwords
- [ ] `.env` file is NOT in staged changes
- [ ] No files with "credential" or "secret" in name
- [ ] Used environment variables for all credentials

## 🆘 Need Help?

- Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.MD) for detailed guidelines
- Contact hackathon support through mentor channel
- Ask in the hackathon Slack workspace

---

**Remember:** Security is everyone's responsibility. When in doubt, ask for help!

# Weather Dashboard — SDLC Harness Demo

A minimal, self-contained web application built to demonstrate an end-to-end SDLC
workflow using the **SDLC Harness** project.  The app itself is intentionally simple
so that every team member can understand the full codebase in minutes, then use it
to practise branching, committing, reviewing, and tracing changes back to work items.

---

## Purpose

This application serves as the **demo artefact** for the SDLC Harness IBM Hackathon
project.  It is not a production weather service; it uses deterministic mock data so
that the same city name always produces the same result, making demo walkthroughs
repeatable without an API key or network connection.

---

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Application shell — semantic HTML, accessible landmarks and form |
| `styles.css` | All styling — CSS custom properties, card layout, dark mode, responsive breakpoints |
| `app.js` | All runtime behaviour — mock data, search, validation, loading state, theme toggle |
| `README.md` | This file |
| `tests.md` | Manual test checklist |

---

## Running Locally

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Open **`index.html`** directly in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
   No server, build step, or package manager is required.

```
# macOS / Linux (optional)
open index.html

# Windows (optional)
start index.html
```

---

## Features

- **City search** — Enter any city name and click Search (or press Enter) to see mock
  weather data generated deterministically from the city name.
- **Default result** — "New York" is displayed on first load so the page is never blank.
- **Validation** — An error message is shown when the city field is empty.
- **Loading state** — A brief spinner simulates an async data fetch (300 ms).
- **Light / Dark theme** — Toggle button in the header; selection is persisted in
  `localStorage` across page reloads.
- **Accessible** — Semantic HTML, ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and visible focus
  indicators throughout.
- **Responsive** — Single-column layout on mobile (≤ 600 px), side-by-side header on
  wider screens.

---

## Suggested SDLC Demo Changes

Use these as concrete tasks to walk through branching, committing, reviewing, and
linking changes back to work items in SDLC Harness:

1. **Add a 5-day forecast section** — extend `getMockWeather()` in `app.js` to return
   an array of daily forecasts and add a new card row in `index.html`.

2. **Change temperature units** — add a °C / °F toggle; store the preference in
   `localStorage` alongside the theme.

3. **Stricter city-name validation** — reject inputs that contain numbers or special
   characters; add the regex rule to `handleSearch()` and expand the test checklist.

4. **Write automated unit tests** — create `tests.js` using plain `console.assert`
   calls (no test framework needed) and open it in the browser console to verify
   `getMockWeather()` and `hashString()` behave correctly.

5. **Real API integration** — replace `getMockWeather()` with a `fetch()` call to the
   [Open-Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key required) and handle the
   async response; update `tests.md` to cover network-error states.

6. **Internationalisation** — add a language selector that switches UI strings between
   English and another language using a simple JavaScript object map.

---

## Security

This project follows the IBM Hackathon security template. Before every commit, verify:

- [ ] Reviewed `git diff` for sensitive data
- [ ] No hardcoded API keys or passwords
- [ ] `.env` file is **not** in staged changes
- [ ] No files with "credential" or "secret" in the name
- [ ] All credentials use environment variables

See [SECURITY.MD](SECURITY.MD) for full guidelines.

# sdlc-harness MVP — Task List

## Priority Legend

- **P0** — required for the MVP demo. Nothing else matters until these work end-to-end.
- **P1** — stretch. Build only if time remains after every P0 item is solid.
- **P2** — explicitly out of scope for this demo. Listed so it isn't forgotten later, not so it gets built now.

## Scope Decisions

- **GitLab hosting:** self-hosted GitLab CE via Docker (confirmed). This is heavier than a hosted alternative — budget real time and RAM for it, and get the smoke test green before building anything on top.
- **Agent tiering:** P0 = Acceptance-criteria drafting, Ambiguity detection, Dependency suggestion, State-transition. P1 = Test-coverage linkage (hardest to seed convincingly with fake data in a live demo — hold back unless the four P0 agents and the demo loop are already solid).
- **Plumbing reuse:** the MCP server skeleton, GitLab REST client, tool-registry pattern, and Bob-config merge/install pattern from the earlier `bob-devops-kit` recreation plan are reused as engineering scaffolding (Section 2A below). Its generic skill set — `backlog-hygiene`, `work-item-optimizer`, `sprint-worker`, `hierarchy-scaffolding`, `code-review`, `formatting-compliance-audit`, `project-researcher` — and its coding-guidelines engine (`guidelines-init/search/status/validate`) solve a **different, adjacent problem** (a general-purpose GitLab coding-assistant kit). They are explicitly **out of scope (P2)** for sdlc-harness and should not be built here.

## Recommended build order (critical path)

Section 1 (infra) → Section 2A (plumbing) → Section 2B (P0 agents + onboarding + review UX) → Section 3 (config/wiring) → Section 4 (onboarding runbook + seed data) → Section 5 (demo plan). Do not start Section 2B until Section 2A's smoke test is green.

---

## 1. Infrastructure: GitLab Docker Environment

1. **GitLab container setup** `[P0]` — author a `docker-compose.yml` that spins up a GitLab CE instance with persistent volumes for config, logs, and data; document the minimum host requirements.
2. **GitLab initial configuration** `[P0]` — script the root password seed, disable sign-ups, create a dedicated `sdlc-harness-demo` group and project via the GitLab API on first boot.
3. **Demo website container** `[P0]` — add a second service to `docker-compose.yml` for a minimal static website (e.g. nginx serving a single HTML page) that represents the "project under governance."
4. **Networking & reverse proxy** `[P1]` — configure an nginx or Traefik reverse proxy so GitLab and the demo site are reachable on named local hostnames (e.g. `gitlab.local`, `demo.local`) without port clashes. Plain `localhost:<port>` links work fine for a single demo run — only build this if time allows.
5. **Security hardening** `[P0]` — confirm no credentials anywhere in source; confirm `.gitignore` coverage for env-files; confirm docs state GitLab credentials come from a runtime env-file only.
6. **Smoke-test script** `[P0]` — write a shell script that validates the full stack is healthy (GitLab readiness endpoint, demo site HTTP 200) and can be run after `docker compose up`. Gate: don't start Section 2 until this passes.

---

## 2A. Plumbing: MCP Server & GitLab Tooling

Reused engineering scaffolding only — not the adjacent generic coding-assistant kit (see Scope Decisions).

7. **MCP server package scaffold** `[P0]` — Node.js + TypeScript package (`package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `build`/`start`/`smoke` scripts), a shared `ToolDefinition` type (description, zod args, `execute(args, ctx)`) used by every tool.
8. **GitLab REST client** `[P0]` — `gitlab-client.ts` wrapping the Issues, Merge Requests, and Labels endpoints via a PAT-based client.
9. **Env loading** `[P0]` — `env.ts` reads GitLab PAT/host/project from a configurable, gitignored env-file path; never overrides existing env vars or logs values.
10. **Tool registry + server glue** `[P0]` — `tools.ts` registry, `index.ts` (creates an `McpServer`, registers each tool, connects `StdioServerTransport`, stays silent on stderr unless a debug flag is set).
11. **GitLab issue reader/writer tools** `[P0]` — `gitlab-issue-reader` (issues, labels, state) and `gitlab-issue-writer` (create/update with duplicate detection). This is the shared read/write surface every one of the five agents calls.
12. **GitLab MR reader/writer tool** `[P0]` — needed for the state-transition agent's "MR merged → suggest In Review" trigger and for the dependency-suggestion agent to see related work.
13. **`work-item-format` tool** `[P0]` — canonical issue-formatting standard (title conventions, description structure, Given-When-Then acceptance criteria) that the agents defer to when drafting AC or rewriting descriptions.
14. **Bob global-config merge pattern** `[P0]` — reuse the MERGE-ONLY handling for `custom_modes.yaml` and `mcp.json` so installing the skill doesn't clobber an existing Bob config on the demo machine.
15. **`install.sh`** `[P1]` — idempotent installer copying skill/rules/config into `~/.bob`. Nice for repeatability across machines; for a single demo box, manual one-time install is fine.
16. **End-to-end plumbing validation** `[P0]` — `npm install && npm run build && npm run smoke`; confirm all registered tools respond before building agents on top. Gate: don't start Section 2B until this passes.

**Explicitly excluded (P2, different product):** `guidelines-init/search/status/validate` (coding-style guidelines engine — unrelated to work-item governance), the generic `🛠 Engineer` TDD mode and its `rules-engineer/*`, and the generic skills `backlog-hygiene`, `work-item-optimizer`, `sprint-worker`, `hierarchy-scaffolding`, `code-review`, `formatting-compliance-audit`, `project-researcher`.

---

## 2B. sdlc-harness Skill & Agents (the actual product)

17. **Skill scaffold** `[P0]` — create the `SKILL.md` file for the `sdlc-harness` Bob skill with correct frontmatter (name, description, triggers) following the Bob skill authoring conventions.
18. **Onboarding conversation flow** `[P0]` — define the guided conversation steps that collect project management tool type (GitLab Issues for the demo), project URL, work item types, workflow states, **and transition rules**; document the expected input/output for each step.
19. **Work item template baseline** `[P0]` — author industry best-practice templates (User Story, Bug, Task, Epic) as structured prompts the skill applies when creating or reviewing work items.
20. **Acceptance criteria agent** `[P0]` — detects issues lacking acceptance criteria and drafts them using the work item description and template as context.
21. **Ambiguity detection agent** `[P0]` — flags descriptions with vague language and proposes concrete rewrites.
22. **Dependency suggestion agent** `[P0]` — scans open issues for semantic overlap and proposes `relates-to` / `blocks` links.
23. **State transition agent** `[P0]` — monitors issue state and proposes the correct next transition based on activity signals (e.g. MR merged → suggest "In Review").
24. **Test coverage linkage agent** `[P1]` — cross-references issues with test files or test plan items and flags uncovered work items. Stretch: hold back until the four P0 agents and demo loop are proven.
25. **Human review interface** `[P0]` — define the Bob interaction pattern by which a developer reviews, approves, edits, or overrides an agent suggestion in natural language without leaving Bob.
26. **Suggestion telemetry** `[P0]` — log each agent proposal plus its outcome (accepted / edited / rejected) to a flat file or a GitLab comment thread. Deliberately minimal — no dashboard — but it's the only concrete hook into the problem statement's "Measuring Success" section (backlog quality / trust / time saved) and lets the demo cite a real acceptance-rate number.

## 3. Agent & Skill Configuration

30. **Agent orchestration design** `[P0]` — document how the four P0 agents (plus where the P1 test-coverage agent would slot in) are triggered (event-driven vs. scheduled poll), how they share context, and how conflicts between agent suggestions are surfaced to the user.
31. **Skill unit tests** `[P1]` — write test cases covering the onboarding flow, each agent's happy path, and the override/rejection path using mock GitLab API responses. Do one manual happy-path pass first; formalize into tests if time remains.

Save them into a repo folder (e.g. `docs/bob-sessions/`) as the build progresses — don't try to reconstruct these retroactively at submission time.

# Problem Statement & Solution

## The Problem

Software teams adopt SDLC processes, but the discipline required to maintain them consistently breaks down in practice. The culprit is friction. Work items accumulate across sprints with missing acceptance criteria, broken dependency links, and descriptions that mean different things to different contributors. Reporting becomes unreliable, traceability gaps create audit risk, and handoffs require costly manual reconciliation.

Existing tools like Jira or Azure DevOps can enforce structural rules such as required fields and blocked transitions, but they cannot reason about the quality of content. A field can be filled in and still be wrong. No current toolchain proactively closes that gap.

## The Solution: sdlc-harness

sdlc-harness is a Bob skill that puts a team of WatsonX AI agents inside the developer's existing workflow to govern work item quality throughout the entire SDLC, before problems reach the backlog.

Target users are software development teams of any size who use a project management tool (Jira, Azure DevOps, GitHub Projects) and want consistent, traceable work items without adding overhead.

A developer or project lead starts a guided onboarding conversation with the sdlc-harness skill inside Bob. In minutes, with no admin configuration or pipeline setup, the skill learns the team's project management tool, work item types, workflow states, and transition rules. Industry best-practice templates are applied as a baseline. From that point, WatsonX agents monitor the project continuously, drafting missing acceptance criteria, flagging ambiguous descriptions, suggesting dependency links, verifying test coverage relationships, and proposing state transitions before a human would notice the gap. Developers review, approve, or override suggestions through natural language inside Bob, without switching context.

## Why It Is New

Most governance tools are reactive. They flag a missing field after a developer has already committed a half-formed work item. sdlc-harness works the other way: agents act first, proposing well-formed work items that conform to the team's own templates, so the developer's job is reviewing good work rather than doing rote work. Onboarding takes minutes with no DevOps setup, removing the barrier that causes most teams to skip governance tooling entirely.

## Measuring Success

Success is visible in three places. First, backlog quality: fewer work items missing acceptance criteria, fewer vague descriptions reaching active development, fewer broken dependency links surfacing during audits or handoffs, and fewer stories or bugs transitioning to Done without a corresponding test link. Second, trust: if developers accept more agent suggestions over time rather than editing or rejecting them, the system is learning team conventions and earning its place. If the acceptance rate stagnates, the agents are adding noise instead of removing it. Third, time: how much less of each sprint do developers and product managers spend manually cleaning up work items? How quickly can a team produce a traceable, audit-ready picture of a release? Those are the exact costs named above, and they should be shrinking sprint over sprint.
